paras: The attempted lynching of Andrew Dinwiddie took place at Paris, Texas, on August 17, 1905, when a mob took Dinwiddie, a Black man accused of trying to assault a white girl, from officers and prepared to hang him in the public square. County Judge Love talked the crowd into returning him to the sheriff, and three days later a grand jury declined to indict him and he was released. The wire story of a mob turned back by a judge's speech ran across the South, and Texas editors later pointed to the case as a near-lynching of an innocent man.

According to the San Antonio Daily Light, Miss Daisy Collins, daughter of E. P. Collins, woke at about 4 a.m. to find a tall man beside her bed, screamed, and saw him escape barefoot through a window, leaving his hat behind. Her age was given as 17 in the wire and the San Antonio account, 15 in the St. Louis Republic, and 18 in a Texas dispatch printed in Bryan. Police followed tracks to a cabin, where a man fled out the back while an officer fired at him.

Sheriff Carpenter and Marshal Minton arrested Dinwiddie that morning in a corn field south of town, where he was pulling fodder. He said he came from near Clarksville and had slept in a cabin a few blocks from the Collins home, and he denied his guilt. Collins was reported to have identified him, and several people said the hat left behind was his.

A committee of citizens demanded the prisoner, and the sheriff promised a special grand jury. In the afternoon a mob overpowered the officers and took Dinwiddie to a bandstand in the square, where several ropes were ready. The Republic's correspondent put the crowd at about 1,400 and wrote that a rope had already been placed around his neck. In the San Antonio account, the hanging was held off only until Collins could identify him in front of the crowd.

Before that happened, Judge Love climbed onto a wagon and urged the crowd to wait for full proof. The terms of the return varied by account: a 24-hour wait in the wire, a promise to hand him back after 24 hours if proved guilty in San Antonio, and a speedy trial in St. Louis. He was taken back to jail, and the acting mayor closed the saloons for three hours.

After about a day of deliberation, the grand jury reported "no bill" and Dinwiddie was released. Jurors traced his movements from Clarksville, and citizens of Red River County testified that he was a "hard-working, peaceable negro." The Republic reported that he had been "severely bruised and beaten" by the mob and that the grand jury had turned to investigating the mob's leaders.

Coverage came only from white papers, and the Black papers searched did not carry the case. The Associated Press wire, which spelled his name "Dimvidder," ran on August 18 in Louisville, Montgomery, Birmingham and Pensacola and later in South Carolina's Bamberg Herald. Its headlines treated the accusation as settled: the Pensacola Journal's read "Mob Takes Texas Ravisher From Sheriff," and the Montgomery Advertiser's called him a "Rapist in Hands of Mob." The Texas dispatch in the Bryan Morning Eagle and Palestine Daily Herald called him a "Black Brute" while still noting the doubt about his identity.

In Texas, the Bryan Morning Eagle praised Judge Love's speech for stopping "the lynchers" but called Dinwiddie "the negro assaulter". The St. Louis Republic credited "sober-minded citizens" and remarked that the crime alleged was one "generally considered to deserve lynching" in the South. Only the Texas follow-ups reported his release, and on August 22 the Eagle wrote that he had been proven "an innocent man" and that lynching was "a crime."

Accounts differ on how he was taken: the Republic says the mob marched to the jail, while the San Antonio paper says a boy found his "hiding place" and officers were overpowered. Accounts also differ on why the mob relented, with the Republic saying the leaders were convinced there was no conclusive evidence and the Bryan dispatch citing doubt about his identity.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Andrew Dinwiddie
bases: A mob took the accused man from officers and prepared to hang him in the public square before a judge's appeal stopped it, an attempted lynching (A2, A3, A1).

A mob of three or more seized him illegally from officers to punish an alleged attempted assault, but he was returned to the sheriff alive and later released (A2, A3, A11, A12); no one was killed, so this was an attempted lynching.

The Associated Press wire (A1), a St. Louis Republic special (A3), a separate Texas dispatch (A4) and the San Antonio Daily Light's account (A2) agree that a mob took the man from officers and was turned back by County Judge Love.

accounts.label: Associated Press wire
accounts.gist: A mob took 'Andrew Dimvidder' from the sheriff and was about to lynch him when Judge Love pleaded for full proof; the mob agreed to wait 24 hours and returned him.

accounts.label: San Antonio Daily Light account
accounts.gist: A mob overpowered officers, dragged him to the bandstand with ropes ready, and waited for Collins to identify him; Love's appeal won his return on a promise that he would be handed back after 24 hours if proved guilty.

accounts.label: St. Louis Republic special
accounts.gist: About 1,400 people took him from the jail and put a rope around his neck; Love convinced the leaders there was no conclusive evidence and promised a speedy trial.

accounts.label: Texas dispatch ('Saved by Scream')
accounts.gist: Collins was positive the right man was caught and a hat was identified as his, but slight doubt about identity restrained the mob; he denied guilt.

accounts.label: Grand jury result
accounts.gist: The grand jury found no evidence to hold him and released him after witnesses vouched for his character.

framing.detail: Southern papers ran the AP wire under headlines such as 'Mob Takes Texas Ravisher From Sheriff' and 'Rapist in Hands of Mob Saved by Justice's Speech'.
The 'Saved by Scream' dispatch called him a 'Black Brute' while noting doubt about his identity.
The St. Louis Republic's editorial credited 'sober-minded citizens' but described the alleged crime as one the South thought deserved lynching.
The Bryan Morning Eagle first praised Judge Love while calling the accused 'the negro assaulter', then after the no bill called lynching 'a crime' and the man innocent.

conflicts.note: The Texas accounts and the Republic agree on Dinwiddie; 'Dimvidder' is the wire's spelling and 'Androg' looks like an OCR error.
No account is clearly better evidence.
